definition: Of work: produced entirely by a machine yet presented under a human name; ghostwritten by something that was never alive.
etymology: From ghostwriter (one who writes under another’s name — a ghost in this sense since 1884) + wrought (archaic past participle of work). The second member of the promptwrought family: wrought marks the making, ghost marks the missing maker. Both halves have moved under the word. Ghost is Old English gāst, ‘breath, spirit’ — the thing that animates a body, long before it was the thing that haunts a house once the body has gone. The ghost in ghostwriter was always the first kind: a living person who agreed to stay out of sight. The ghost in ghostwrought is the second. Nobody is out of sight, because nobody was there. Wrought is the honest half: the old word for worked, the iron beaten into shape, the making with a hand visibly in it. Put ghost in front of it and the hand goes.
in_use: The essay was ghostwrought — his name, its voice, nobody home.
the_case: Ghostwritten was nearly the word, and the gap between them is the point. A ghostwritten book has a ghost: a person, paid, who did the work and agreed to vanish — and who could still tell you what the third chapter meant. Ghostwrought takes the person away. The name on the cover did not write it, and neither did anyone else. It is an adjective because it describes the work, not the author; a piece can be ghostwrought without anyone quite deciding to deceive. What it accuses is exact: not the machine, which did as it was asked, and not the use of one, but the byline — the one thing on the page a human touched, and the only promise the page still makes. Beside the masthead word it draws the volume’s cleanest line: one adjective for machine work with the hand left showing, one for machine work with the hand taken away.
seo_title: ghostwrought — a human name on machine-made work
seo_description: The name is his. The voice is not. Ghostwrought names writing produced entirely by a machine and signed by a person: ghostwritten by something that was never alive.
